hook

A nineteen-year-old dropped out of Stanford with a promise that could change medicine forever. One tiny drop of blood from your finger, and a small box would run hundreds of tests in minutes. No needles. No waiting. Investors handed her almost a billion dollars. Her company was worth nine billion. People called her the next Steve Jobs. There was just one problem. The box did not work. And it all came crashing down because two young employees decided to tell the truth. This is the story of Elizabeth Holmes.
child

Washington, the nineteen nineties. Elizabeth was a quiet, serious girl with a giant ambition. When a relative asked what she wanted to be when she grew up, she did not say doctor, or astronaut. She said, a billionaire. She loved stories about great inventors. And she was terrified of needles. That fear would become the idea that made her famous.
stanford

In 2002 she went to Stanford University to study chemical engineering. But a classroom felt far too slow. At just nineteen, she took the money her parents had saved for her education, and she dropped out. She started a company in a tiny office. She called it Theranos, a mix of the words therapy and diagnosis.
promise

Her pitch was simple, and brilliant. Today, a blood test means a needle, several tubes of blood, and days of waiting. Theranos would need only a few drops from a fingertip. A machine the size of a printer would run hundreds of tests, cheap and fast. She named it the Edison, after the great inventor. If it worked, it would change healthcare for everyone on Earth.
image

And she looked the part. She wore a black turtleneck every single day, just like Steve Jobs. She spoke in a deep, calm voice. She barely blinked. She worked almost every day of the year, and she expected the same from everyone around her. Silicon Valley fell in love.
money

The money poured in. Rupert Murdoch. The Walton family of Walmart. The DeVos family. In total, Theranos raised around nine hundred million dollars. Her board was full of legends. Two former secretaries of state, Henry Kissinger and George Shultz, and a future secretary of defense, General James Mattis. Then Walgreens signed a deal to put Theranos blood tests inside its pharmacies.
peak

By 2014, Theranos was worth nine billion dollars, and Elizabeth owned about half of it. At thirty, she was the youngest self-made woman billionaire in the world. She was on magazine covers, on giant stages, and on live TV. Everyone wanted to know her secret.
secret

But inside the building, the secret was ugly. The Edison did not work. It gave wrong results, and it could only run a handful of tests. So, behind closed doors, Theranos ran most blood samples on ordinary machines bought from other companies, and hid them from visitors. Her number two, Sunny Balwani, ran the labs with fear. He was also her secret boyfriend. Workers who asked questions were watched, threatened, or fired.
whistle

Two young employees could not stay silent. Erika Cheung, and Tyler Shultz, the grandson of her own board member, saw patients getting wrong results. They went to the regulators. Then a reporter named John Carreyrou, at the Wall Street Journal, got a tip and started digging. Theranos sent lawyers after him and his sources. He published anyway.
fall

October 2015. The article hit like a bomb. Inspectors walked into the lab and found serious problems. Walgreens ended the partnership. Two years of test results were thrown out. Forbes changed her fortune from four and a half billion dollars, to zero. In 2018, the company shut down, and Elizabeth was charged with fraud.
end

In January 2022, a jury found her guilty of defrauding investors. She was sentenced to more than eleven years in federal prison. Sunny Balwani got almost thirteen. Today she is still serving her sentence in Texas, and she has asked for a pardon. The girl who wanted to be a billionaire got her wish. Then she lost it all, because a box that could not work was sold as a miracle. For more stories like this, subscribe to Rise and Ruin.
